title: Marketing Listings & Advertising Compliance
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: An agent posts a listing photo, price, and her personal cell number to her Instagram account, with no brokerage identification anywhere in the post. This is most likely:
options: Acceptable, because social media is personal rather than commercial
A blind ad, because it fails to reveal the advertiser is a licensee acting through a broker
A RESPA violation
Acceptable if her bio mentions she is an agent
rationales: The DRE treats social media as solicitation material; the platform's informality is irrelevant.
Correct. Advertising property without identifying the licensee's status and responsible broker is a blind ad and is prohibited.
RESPA governs settlement service referrals, not advertising identification.
A bio mention does not cure identification missing from the material advertising the property.

questions.stem: Which listing phrase presents BOTH a fair housing problem and a separate factual-representation risk?
options: Updated kitchen with quartz counters
Quiet, safe family neighborhood
Detached two-car garage
Corner lot with mature landscaping
rationales: This describes a property feature objectively.
Correct. 'Family' implicates familial status, while 'safe' is an unverifiable claim about crime that creates misrepresentation exposure independently.
This describes a physical feature.
This describes the lot objectively.

options: Prohibited in California
Permitted, but must be disclosed as virtually staged
Permitted without disclosure if the staging is realistic
Permitted only for vacant land
rationales: Virtual staging is widely used and lawful.
Correct. Virtual staging must be clearly labeled; an unlabeled staged image misrepresents the property's actual condition and scale.
Realism makes an undisclosed alteration more misleading, not less.
Virtual staging is used for improved property, not land.

questions.stem: An agent virtually stages a room, placing a rug over an area of damaged flooring, and does not label the photo. The most serious problem is that the image:
options: Used furniture the seller does not own
Concealed a property condition a buyer would want to see
Was taken with a wide-angle lens
Was not credited to the photographer
rationales: Depicting furniture the seller does not own is ordinary staging and is not itself the problem.
Correct. Beyond the labeling failure, placing a virtual element over a defect moves the conduct toward active concealment of a material condition.
Lens choice raises separate scale concerns but is not what happened here.
Attribution is a copyright matter, unrelated to concealment.

questions.stem: Which statement in listing copy is lawful puffing rather than a representation of fact?
options: Approximately 2,180 square feet
Permitted bonus room
Charming curb appeal
Zoned for commercial use
rationales: Square footage is verifiable fact and a frequent source of misrepresentation claims.
Permit status is verifiable and must never be stated without seeing the permit.
Correct. 'Charming' is subjective opinion no reasonable buyer relies on as fact.
Zoning is verifiable fact.

questions.stem: An agent repeats a 2,450 sq ft figure from a prior listing; the assessor shows 2,180, and part of the difference is an unpermitted patio enclosure. The agent's exposure is:
options: None, because the figure came from a prior listing
Misrepresentation, because innocent misstatement of a material fact can support rescission or damages
Limited to a DRE warning letter
None, if the buyer had the opportunity to measure
rationales: Repeating an unverified figure is not verification and provides no defense.
Correct. Even innocent misrepresentation of a material fact can support rescission or damages, and the unpermitted enclosure is separately material and should have been disclosed.
Civil liability and license discipline both remain available; a warning is not the ceiling.
A buyer's opportunity to verify does not excuse an affirmative misstatement by the agent.

questions.stem: The safest way to advertise square footage is to:
options: State the figure without qualification
Cite the source and recommend buyer verification
Round up to the nearest hundred
Omit square footage entirely
rationales: An unqualified figure is an affirmative representation the agent must be able to support.
Correct. Attributing the figure to its source — assessor, appraisal, or builder — and recommending buyer verification is the standard protective practice.
Rounding up overstates the property and compounds the risk.
Omitting a material marketing detail disserves the seller when a qualified statement is available.

questions.stem: Which advertising phrase constitutes source of income discrimination in California?
options: Cash offers preferred
No Section 8
Conventional financing welcome
Seller will consider all offers
rationales: Preferring cash concerns transaction certainty, not a protected characteristic.
Correct. Source of income is protected under California law, and refusing housing vouchers in advertising is a clear violation.
Noting acceptable financing types does not exclude a protected source of income.
This states openness and excludes no one.

questions.stem: Listing photographs are typically owned by:
options: The listing agent automatically
The photographer, unless the agreement transfers rights
The seller, as owner of the property
The MLS
rationales: Paying for photos does not by itself transfer copyright.
Correct. Photographs are copyrighted works owned by the photographer absent a written transfer or license — which is why agents need a written license covering their intended uses.
Owning the property does not create copyright in images of it.
MLS submission grants usage rights within the MLS framework but does not transfer ownership.

questions.stem: An agent who represented the buyer places a 'SOLD' rider bearing her name on a property she did not list. This is:
options: Standard practice for the buyer's agent
Misleading, because it implies a listing role she did not have
Permitted with the buyer's consent
Permitted if the sign is removed within a week
rationales: Sign riders on a listing belong to the listing broker.
Correct. Advertising a sale in a way that implies a role the agent did not have is misleading; 'Just sold — represented the buyer' would be accurate.
The buyer cannot authorize a misleading representation about the agent's role.
Duration does not cure a misleading implication.

questions.stem: Displaying another broker's listings on an agent's website is generally permitted through IDX, provided the agent:
options: Removes the listing broker's name to avoid confusion
Complies with MLS attribution requirements
Obtains the seller's written consent
Pays the listing broker a display fee
rationales: Removing the listing broker's identification is precisely the violation attribution rules prevent.
Correct. IDX permits display of other participants' listings subject to attribution requirements identifying the listing broker.
Seller consent flows through the listing broker's MLS participation, not individual permission.
IDX display does not involve a per-listing payment to the listing broker.

questions.stem: An agent digitally removes overhead power lines from a listing photograph. This is:
options: Acceptable image enhancement
A misrepresentation of the property's actual condition
Acceptable if disclosed only to the buyer's agent
Acceptable because power lines are outside the property line
rationales: Removing a real feature goes beyond enhancement into altering what the property is.
Correct. Editing out power lines, neighboring structures, or other real conditions misrepresents the property, distinct from disclosed virtual staging.
Selective disclosure to one party does not cure a misleading public advertisement.
A condition visible from and affecting the property is material regardless of where the poles sit.

questions.stem: AI-generated or AI-enhanced listing imagery should be treated:
options: As ordinary photography requiring no special handling
The same as virtual staging — permitted, clearly labeled, and never used to conceal a condition
As prohibited under all circumstances
As acceptable only for exterior shots
rationales: Imagery that does not depict the property as it is cannot be presented as ordinary photography.
Correct. If an image does not show the property as it actually exists, it must be disclosed as an alteration and must never mask a defect.
Enhancement is not categorically prohibited; undisclosed misrepresentation is.
The concern is accuracy, not which elevation is depicted.

questions.stem: A licensee's website must display licensee and broker identification:
options: Only on the contact page
On pages a consumer may land on, not buried in a single interior page
Only if the site advertises specific listings
Only in the site's terms of use
rationales: Consumers arrive on many pages directly from search and social links.
Correct. Identification must be present where a consumer encounters the solicitation, not hidden on one interior page.
The identification obligation attaches to solicitation generally, not only to listing pages.
Legal boilerplate is not where required identification belongs.

questions.stem: An agent advertises 'Sold 12 homes last year,' but 12 was the team's total and the agent personally represented 4. The claim is:
options: Acceptable industry shorthand
Misleading, because production claims must accurately reflect the agent's own role
Acceptable if the team name appears nearby
Acceptable because team production is shared
rationales: Ambiguity that inflates an agent's record is not shorthand; it is a misrepresentation.
Correct. Advertised production statistics must be accurate and not misleading about the agent's personal involvement.
Proximity of a team name does not clarify that the agent personally handled four transactions.
Shared team effort does not permit an individual to claim the team's total as personal production.

questions.stem: Marketing imagery that consistently depicts only one demographic group can:
options: Never raise legal concerns, since images make no statements
Signal an unlawful preference under fair housing law
Be cured by adding the Equal Housing Opportunity logo
Be justified as reflecting the neighborhood's composition
rationales: Images communicate preference as effectively as words and are treated accordingly.
Correct. Advertising imagery indicating a preference for or against protected groups is a documented enforcement theory.
The logo is required but does not cure imagery that signals a preference.
Reflecting neighborhood composition is not a defense to advertising that signals who is welcome.

questions.stem: Describing a property as 'walking distance to St. Anne's' raises a concern under:
options: Truth in Lending
Fair housing law, because it may signal a religious preference
RESPA
The statute of frauds
rationales: TILA governs credit cost disclosure.
Correct. Naming a religious institution as a landmark can indicate a religious preference; a neutral proximity reference is the safer construction.
RESPA governs settlement service referrals.
The statute of frauds concerns which contracts must be written.

questions.stem: The single best test to apply before publishing any listing copy or social post is:
options: Does it sound professional?
Does it describe the property rather than the people?
Is it under the character limit?
Does it mention the price?
rationales: Tone does not detect fair housing problems.
Correct. Nearly every advertising fair housing violation fails this one test, and applying it consistently also produces better marketing copy.
Length has no bearing on compliance.
Price disclosure is unrelated to the fair housing risk in copy.
